name: Monsters (hard version)
description: This is the hard version of the problem. In this version, you need to find the answer for every prefix of the monster array. In a computer game, you are fighting against $$$n$$$ monsters. Monster number $$$i$$$ has $$$a_i$$$ health points, all $$$a_i$$$ are integers. A monster is alive while it has at least $$$1$$$ health point. You can cast spells of two types: Deal $$$1$$$ damage to any single alive monster of your choice. Deal $$$1$$$ damage to all alive monsters. If at least one monster dies (ends up with $$$0$$$ health points) as a result of this action, then repeat it (and keep repeating while at least one monster dies every time). Dealing $$$1$$$ damage to a monster reduces its health by $$$1$$$. Spells of type 1 can be cast any number of times, while a spell of type 2 can be cast at most once during the game. For every $$$k = 1, 2, \ldots, n$$$, answer the following question. Suppose that only the first $$$k$$$ monsters, with numbers $$$1, 2, \ldots, k$$$, are present in the game. What is the smallest number of times you need to cast spells of type 1 to kill all $$$k$$$ monsters?
input_specification: Each test contains multiple test cases. The first line contains the number of test cases $$$t$$$ ($$$1 \le t \le 10^4$$$). The description of the test cases follows. Each test case consists of two lines. The first line contains a single integer $$$n$$$ ($$$1 \le n \le 2 \cdot 10^5$$$) — the number of monsters. The second line contains $$$n$$$ integers $$$a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n$$$ ($$$1 \le a_i \le n$$$) — monsters' health points. It is guaranteed that the sum of $$$n$$$ over all test cases does not exceed $$$2 \cdot 10^5$$$.
output_specification: For each test case, print $$$n$$$ integers. The $$$k$$$-th of these integers must be equal to the smallest number of times you need to cast spells of type 1 to kill all $$$k$$$ monsters, if only monsters with numbers $$$1, 2, \ldots, k$$$ are present in the game.
approach_summary: Build a Segment Tree over the array. Implement point update and associative range query operations in O(log N) time per query.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 1784C — Monsters (hard version) [57. Segment Tree (Point Update Range Query)]
topic_editorial.summary: Range queries and updates via Segment Tree.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: The query operation is associative (e.g., sum, min, max, gcd). Any contiguous range $[L, R]$ can be decomposed into at most $O(\log N)$ canonical dyadic intervals represented by nodes in a binary tree.
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: Tree Construction
We build a binary segment tree over array $A[1..N]$.
Each node covers a segment $[L, R]$. If $L = R$, the node stores $A[L]$. Otherwise:
$$\text{node.val} = \text{combine}(\text{left\_child.val}, \text{right\_child.val})$$

### Step 2: Point / Range Updates
To update position $pos$ with value $val$:
- Traverse down to the leaf node $[pos, pos]$.
- Update leaf value.
- Recompute ancestor values on the way back up in $O(\log N)$ time.

### Step 3: Range Query Processing
To query the associative aggregate on range $[qL, qR]$:
- If current segment $[L, R]$ is completely within $[qL, qR]$, return node value.
- If disjoint, return identity element.
- Otherwise, split and return $\text{combine}(\text{query}(left), \text{query}(right))$.
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}((N + Q) \log N)$
  Building the segment tree takes $\mathcal{O}(N)$. Each point/range query and update traverses at most $4 \log N$ tree nodes, requiring $\mathcal{O}(\log N)$ time per query.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  A standard binary segment tree requires at most $4N$ nodes to represent elements up to index $N$.
